Series::xlogy¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::xlogy(const Series& other) const -> Series
Series& Series::xlogy_(const Series& other)
Series& Series::xlogy_(const Series& rhs) const
Series& Series::xlogy_(double rhs) const

What It Does¶

xlogy() computes a * log(b) elementwise, with one deliberate exception: when a is 0 the result is 0, even if log(b) is -inf or undefined.

The plain product a * b.log() gets this case wrong. At a = 0, b = 0 it evaluates 0 * log(0) = 0 * (-inf) = NaN. But the limit of a * log(b) as a -> 0 is 0, and that is the value nearly every application wants.

The name is read “x log y”. It shows up wherever a weighted log appears and some weights are exactly zero:

  • entropy, -sum p * log(p), where some p are 0

  • cross-entropy and KL divergence between distributions with zeros

  • log-likelihoods of count data where some counts are 0

xlogy() lets you write those sums directly without masking the zero terms by hand.

Parameters¶

other (const Series&)

The value b whose logarithm is taken. Broadcasts against the receiver.

Returns¶

Series or Series& a * log(b), except 0 wherever a == 0. A NaN in b still propagates. xlogy_() writes the result back into the receiver.

Gradient¶

xlogy() is differentiable:

d/da xlogy(a, b) = log(b)
d/db xlogy(a, b) = a / b

Because the a == 0 result is pinned to the constant 0, the gradient through those positions is 0 for both operands — it does not carry the log(b) term there. Everywhere else the rule is the ordinary product rule.

In-Place Form¶

xlogy_() is the in-place sibling of xlogy(): it computes the same result and writes it back into self directly — mutating it (and any other handle sharing the same storage) instead of allocating a new Series — then returns a reference to self.

Despite being declared const at the call site — a quirk of how this method’s wrapper is generated, not a promise that self is left unchanged — xlogy_() genuinely mutates the series it’s called on.

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 2.0}, {3});
auto y = pluss::make_series({1.0, 1.0, 1.0}, {3});

x.xlogy_(y);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

auto x = pluss::make_series({0.0, 1.0, 2.0}, {3});
x.xlogy_(1.0);
std::cout << x;

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 0, 0]

Examples¶

Example 1. A zero weight zeroes the term even when log(b) is -inf.

auto a = pluss::make_series({0.0, 2.0, 3.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({0.0, 4.0, 8.0});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, a.xlogy(b));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0.0000, 2.7726, 6.2383]

The first term is 0 (not NaN). The others are 2 * log 4 and 3 * log 8.

Example 2. A non-zero weight against b = 0 is still -inf; only a == 0 is special-cased.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({2.0}).xlogy(pluss::make_series({0.0})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[-inf]

Example 3. A NaN in b propagates regardless of a.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({0.0}).xlogy(pluss::make_series({std::nan("")})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[1], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=[nan]

Example 4. The gradient is (log(b), a / b) on the non-zeroed positions.

auto a = pluss::make_series({2.0, 3.0});
auto b = pluss::make_series({4.0, 5.0});
a.tracks_slope_(true);
b.tracks_slope_(true);

a.xlogy(b).sum().reverse();

std::cout << "da=" << a.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "db=" << b.sensitivity() << "\n";

Output¶

da=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1.3862944, 1.6094379]
db=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0.5, 0.6]

da is log 4 and log 5; db is 2/4 and 3/5.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • Only a == 0 is special-cased. a slightly nonzero with b == 0 still gives -inf.

  • A NaN in b propagates even when a == 0.

  • Floating-point inputs.

  • xlogy() is not symmetric: a.xlogy(b) is a * log(b), not b * log(a).

Summary¶

xlogy(a, b) is a * log(b) with the convention 0 * log(0) = 0:

  • broadcasts like add()

  • fixes the NaN that the plain product produces at a = b = 0

  • differentiable, gradient (log(b), a / b), and 0 through the pinned positions

See Also¶

  • Series::log: the logarithm xlogy() wraps.

  • Series::mul: the plain product, which does not special-case the zero weight.
